mn-039-p02.plain: A baby quickly pulls back a hand that touches a burning coal. In the same way, someone with right view who slips into a fixable offence quickly confesses it to the Teacher or a wise companion and restrains themselves afterward.
mn-039-p02.core_idea: The wise quickly confess and correct their faults.

mn-041-p01.plain: A fire doesn't plan to burn the fool, yet the fool who attacks it gets burned anyway.
mn-041-p01.core_idea: Attacking what is pure only harms the attacker.

mn-042-p01.plain: There are four kinds of people: those who torment themselves, those who torment others, those who do both, and those who do neither. The last live without cravings in this life, cooled, blissful, become divine.
mn-042-p01.core_idea: Harming neither self nor others leads to bliss.

mn-043-p01.plain: A noble disciple eats in moderation by reflecting that food is not for fun or looks, but only to sustain the body, avoid harm and support spiritual practice, ending old discomfort without creating new.
mn-043-p01.core_idea: Eat in moderation, only to sustain the practice.

judge.issue: Drops 'means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding'.

mn-044-p01.plain: A man parades through town in a borrowed carriage and jewels, and people think he's rich. When the owners take back their things, he has reason to be upset, because none of it was ever his.
mn-044-p01.core_idea: Borrowed pleasures can be taken back at any time.

mn-046-p01.plain: The Buddha tells a householder to act only after careful thought, especially since he is well known.

mn-050-p01.plain: Showing Rāhula a little water left in a pot, the Buddha says that's how little of the ascetic's nature remains in those who aren't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie.
mn-050-p01.core_idea: Shameless lying empties out the spiritual life.

mn-050-p02.plain: The Buddha asks Rāhula what a mirror is for; it's for checking your reflection. In the same way, every deed of body, speech and mind should be done only after checking it again and again.
mn-050-p02.core_idea: Check every action as you would a mirror.

mn-051-p01.plain: After acting, check whether the deed harmed yourself or others. If it did, confess it to the Teacher or a wise companion and hold back in future. If it didn't, live in joy and keep training in what is good.
mn-051-p01.core_idea: Review your deeds: confess harm, rejoice in good.

judge.issue: Generalises bodily acts to any act; drops 'unskillful, suffering as its result'.

mn-051-p02.plain: The Buddha tells Rāhula to meditate like the earth. People throw clean and filthy things on it, yet it isn't disgusted; meditating this way, pleasant and unpleasant experiences won't take over his mind.
mn-051-p02.core_idea: Be like the earth, unmoved by clean or foul.

mn-051-p03.plain: Meditate on love and ill will falls away; on compassion and cruelty falls away; on rejoicing and discontent falls away; on equanimity and aversion falls away.
mn-051-p03.core_idea: Each wholesome meditation removes its opposite.

mn-052-p01.plain: A man struck by a poisoned arrow refuses treatment until he learns who shot him, the man's looks and home, and every detail of the bow and arrow. He would die before learning any of it.
mn-052-p01.core_idea: Demanding every answer first can cost your life.

mn-054-p01.plain: When a horse trainer first gets a fine thoroughbred used to the bit, it twists and dodges because it is new to this. But with regular, gradual practice its bad behaviour fades away.

mn-055-p01.plain: A very poor man envies a calm meditating monk and wishes he could go forth. Yet he can't give up even his broken hovel, couch, grain pot and wife, though none is anything special.
mn-055-p01.core_idea: Even poor attachments can bind us strongly.

mn-058-p01.plain: Enlightenment isn't achieved all at once but by gradual training and practice. Someone with faith approaches a teacher, listens, remembers and examines the teachings, strives, and finally sees the ultimate truth with wisdom.

mn-059-p01.plain: Greed is unwholesome and contentment wholesome; hate is unwholesome and love wholesome; delusion is unwholesome and understanding wholesome.
mn-059-p01.core_idea: Contentment, love and understanding overcome greed, hate, delusion.

mn-060-p01.plain: Arguing leads to dispute, dispute to distress, and distress to harm.
mn-060-p01.core_idea: Arguments lead step by step to harm.

mn-061-p01.plain: All feelings, whether pleasant, painful or neutral, are impermanent and arise from conditions; they are bound to end, vanish and fade away.
mn-061-p01.core_idea: Every feeling is impermanent and passes.

mn-061-p03.plain: The Buddha sees beings consumed and burning with craving for sensual pleasure, and doesn't envy them. He knows a satisfaction apart from sensual pleasure that rivals heavenly joy, so he has no wish for the lesser kind.
mn-061-p03.core_idea: A higher joy frees you from envying sensual pleasure.

mn-062-p01.plain: A leper scratches his sores and scorches them over coals; the wounds only get worse, yet he finds some relief in it. Likewise, the more people indulge sensual pleasure, the more their craving burns, though they still find some gratification.
mn-062-p01.core_idea: Indulging craving feeds it, like scratching a wound.

mn-062-p02.plain: Health is the greatest blessing, and extinguishment the greatest happiness.
mn-062-p02.core_idea: Health is the best blessing; extinguishment the best happiness.

mn-069-p01.plain: The senses give sensual pleasure, but beyond it lies a pleasure that rises above the sensual, and that is said to be the best.
mn-069-p01.core_idea: A pleasure beyond the senses is the best.

mn-069-p02.plain: A baby swaddled up to the neck is released from those wrappings as it grows and its senses mature. It knows it is free, and there are no more bonds.
mn-069-p02.core_idea: Growing maturity releases us from our bonds.

mn-071-p01.plain: Four summaries of the teaching: the world is unstable and swept away; it has no shelter or saviour; it has no owner, and you must leave it all behind; it is always wanting, a slave to craving.
mn-071-p01.core_idea: The world is unstable, unprotected, unowned and craving.

mn-072-p01.plain: Friends can't help when you die; heirs take your wealth, and beings fare on by their deeds. Riches, family and kingdom don't follow you, nor buy long life or stop old age. Life is short for all; the fool lies stricken by his own folly, but the wise don't tremble.
mn-072-p01.core_idea: Death takes everything; only the wise stay unshaken.
mn-072-p01.plain_v1: Family and friends can't help you as you die; wealth, children and kingdom stay behind, and beings go on by their deeds. Life is short for all, but only the fool is struck down; the attentive don't tremble.

judge_v1.issue: 'Only the fool is struck down' misreads 'stricken by their own folly'; drops riches can't buy longevity.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Says only the fool is struck; the passage says all feel its touch.

mn-074-p01.plain: The Buddha saw that his extreme self-torment, as severe as anyone's, hadn't brought awakening. Then he remembered entering a blissful first absorption as a boy under a plum tree, and realised that this was the path to awakening.
mn-074-p01.core_idea: Awakening came through gentle absorption, not self-torment.

mn-075-p01.plain: The Buddha saw that beings differ: some have little dust in their eyes, some much; some are easy to teach, some hard. Like lotuses, some stay underwater, some reach the surface, and some rise clear of the water.
mn-075-p01.core_idea: Beings differ in readiness, like lotuses in a pond.

judge.issue: Drops beings who do or don't see danger regarding the next world.

mn-076-p01.plain: The killer Aṅgulimāla asks how the walking Buddha has stopped while he hasn't. The Buddha answers that he has stopped forever by laying aside violence toward all creatures, but Aṅgulimāla can't stop harming living beings.
mn-076-p01.core_idea: True stopping means giving up all violence.

mn-077-p01.plain: Someone who was once careless but became careful, whose bad deeds are replaced by good ones, lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds.
mn-077-p01.core_idea: Turning from bad to good makes a person shine.

mn-077-p02.plain: Irrigators guide water, fletchers straighten arrows and carpenters straighten timber, but the wise tame themselves.

mn-085-p01.plain: You can have full faith in something and it may still be empty and false. And you can lack full faith in something and it may still be true.
mn-085-p01.core_idea: Strong faith doesn't make something true.

mn-085-p02.plain: Striving helps you arrive at the truth. Without striving you won't get there; you reach the truth because you strive.
mn-085-p02.core_idea: You reach the truth by striving.

mn-085-p03.plain: The Buddha says he doesn't tell people to serve everyone, nor no one. Don't serve someone if serving them makes you worse; do serve someone if serving them makes you better.
mn-085-p03.core_idea: Serve those whose service makes you better.

mn-085-p04.plain: The Buddha says that being born into an eminent family, being very beautiful, or being very wealthy does not make you a better or worse person.
mn-085-p04.core_idea: Birth, beauty and wealth don't make you better.

mn-086-p01.plain: There are ways of earning a living that are both profitable and honest. With them you can support your parents, avoid bad deeds and follow the path of goodness.
mn-086-p01.core_idea: Honest work can support family and goodness.

mn-087-p03.plain: You are not a brahmin or a non-brahmin by birth. Your deeds make you a brahmin, and your deeds make you a non-brahmin.
mn-087-p03.core_idea: Your deeds, not your birth, define you.

mn-088-p01.plain: There are five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

mn-090-p01.plain: A man struck by a poisoned arrow has a surgeon cut, probe, extract and cauterise, each step sharply painful. In time the wound heals, and he is healthy, happy, independent and free to go where he likes.
mn-090-p01.core_idea: Painful treatment can lead to lasting health.

mn-091-p01.plain: A mendicant sees that living as they please makes bad qualities grow, while striving hard makes good ones grow, so they strive. Later they no longer need to strive hard, because they have reached the goal they strove for.
mn-091-p01.core_idea: Hard effort is needed only until the goal is reached.

judge.issue: Softens 'strive painfully' to 'strive hard'.

mn-093-p01.plain: If you see that correcting someone would trouble you and hurt them, because they're irritable and stubbornly cling to their views, and you can't turn them toward good, don't underestimate the value of equanimity toward them.
mn-093-p01.core_idea: With some people, equanimity is the wise response.

mn-095-p01.plain: A bronze goblet holds a drink with lovely colour, smell and taste, but it is poisoned. Would someone who wants to live and be happy drink it, knowing it would bring death or deadly suffering?
mn-095-p01.core_idea: Don't drink pleasure you know is poisoned.

mn-095-p02.plain: Sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, false and deceptive. They are made of illusion, and only fools are taken in by them.

judge.issue: 'Lamented by fools' shifted to 'only fools are taken in by them'.

mn-096-p01.plain: Out of compassion the Buddha has done what a caring teacher should. He points Ānanda to the tree roots and empty huts and urges him to meditate, not to be negligent, and not to regret it later.
mn-096-p01.core_idea: The teacher has shown the way; now practise.

mn-096-p02.plain: The Buddha tells a mendicant to eat in moderation, reflecting that food is not for fun or looks but only to sustain the body, avoid harm and support practice, ending old discomfort without creating new.
mn-096-p02.core_idea: Eat in moderation, only to sustain the practice.

judge.issue: Drops 'means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding'.

mn-097-p01.plain: The Buddha didn't praise every kind of meditation. He didn't praise meditating while secretly gripped by desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness or doubt, without understanding how to escape them, and just brooding.
mn-097-p01.core_idea: Meditation that hides inner hindrances isn't praised.

mn-098-p01.plain: A true person gives advice that doesn't hurt themselves, others or both.

mn-098-p02.plain: A true person gives carefully, with their own hand and with thought. They don't give leftovers, and they consider the consequences of their gift.

mn-100-p01.plain: A true person knows that fame doesn't end greed, hate or delusion; anyone who practises the teaching properly deserves honour, famous or not. So they keep their practice to themselves and don't use fame to raise themselves and belittle others.
mn-100-p01.core_idea: Practice, not fame, makes a person worthy.

mn-102-p01.plain: All dangers, perils and hazards come from fools, not from the wise. It's like a fire that starts in a grass hut and burns down even a well-built, sealed house.
mn-102-p01.core_idea: Danger comes from fools, not the wise.

mn-105-p01.plain: Whoever develops mindfulness of the body includes every wholesome quality that leads to realisation, just as picturing the ocean includes all the streams that flow into it.
mn-105-p01.core_idea: Mindfulness of the body contains all the good.

mn-106-p01.plain: A mendicant who loves company and groups doesn't shine and can't easily find the peace of renunciation, seclusion and awakening. One who lives alone, withdrawn from the group, can find these pleasures easily.
mn-106-p01.core_idea: Solitude, not company, brings deeper peace.

mn-107-p01.plain: The Buddha says there isn't a single sight that, when it decays and perishes, wouldn't bring sorrow, pain and distress to someone who desires it.
mn-107-p01.core_idea: Whatever we crave brings sorrow when it fades.

mn-107-p02.plain: The Buddha says he won't coddle his disciples like a potter handling damp, unfired pots. He will correct and push them again and again, and what is solid will stand the test.
mn-107-p02.core_idea: Hard correction reveals what is sound.

mn-109-p01.plain: Someone needing oil heaps sand in a bucket, sprinkles it with water and presses it, but gets no oil, whether they wish for it or not. That is simply the wrong way to get oil.
mn-109-p01.core_idea: The wrong method fails, whatever you wish.

mn-111-p01.plain: Those who keep repeating that someone abused, hit, beat or robbed them never lay their hatred to rest; those who let go of such grudges do. Hatred is never ended by hatred, only by love: this is an ancient teaching.
mn-111-p01.core_idea: Hatred ends not by hatred but by love.

mn-111-p02.plain: If you find a wise, attentive friend, travel with them joyfully and mindfully through every hardship. If not, walk alone like a tusker in the wild; there's no fellowship with fools. Better alone and doing no wrong.
mn-111-p02.core_idea: Better to walk alone than with fools.

mn-112-p01.plain: When a fool rests, their past bad deeds of body, speech and mind settle over them, like the shadow of a great mountain falling over the land in the evening.
mn-112-p01.core_idea: Past wrongdoing weighs on the fool like a shadow.

mn-114-p01.plain: Seeing that grasping is the source of birth and death, those who cling to nothing are freed from both. Happy and safe, at peace in this very life, they have moved beyond all hostility, fear and suffering.
mn-114-p01.core_idea: Letting go of grasping frees you from suffering.

mn-114-p02.plain: Don't run back to the past or anticipate the future; see clearly what is present, and know and foster the unshakable. Work keenly today, for death may come tomorrow and won't bargain. One who meditates tirelessly like this, night and day, has had one fine night, says the peaceful sage.
mn-114-p02.core_idea: Live fully in the present; death won't wait.
mn-114-p02.plain_v1: Don't run back to the past or reach for the future; the past is gone and the future hasn't come. See clearly what is here now. Work keenly today, for death may come tomorrow and can't be bargained with.

judge_v1.issue: Drops 'know the unshakable and foster it' and the tireless meditator who has one fine night.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Drops fostering the unshakable and the meditator who has one fine night.

mn-116-p01.plain: Beings own their deeds and inherit them. Their deeds are their origin, their family and their refuge, and it is deeds that make some beings lower and some higher.
mn-116-p01.core_idea: We are shaped by our deeds.

mn-119-p01.plain: Don't indulge in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, nor in self-torment, which is painful and pointless. Avoiding both extremes, the Buddha found the middle way, which leads to insight, peace, awakening and extinguishment.
mn-119-p01.core_idea: The middle way avoids indulgence and self-torment.

mn-119-p02.plain: Don't speak about people behind their backs, don't speak sharply to their faces, and don't speak in a rush.

mn-120-p01.plain: If what you'd say about someone, behind their back or sharply to their face, is false, don't say it. If true but useless, train yourself not to say it. If true and helpful, know the right time to say it.
mn-120-p01.core_idea: Speak only what is true, useful and timely.

mn-120-p02.plain: Speaking in a rush tires the body, stresses the mind and voice, makes the throat sore and makes words unclear. Speaking unhurriedly avoids all this, and your words are clear and easy to understand.
mn-120-p02.core_idea: Speak slowly to speak clearly and calmly.

mn-120-p03.plain: Don't neglect wisdom, keep to the truth, grow in generosity, and train only for peace.

mn-123-p01.plain: People are purified by their deeds, knowledge, principles, ethical conduct and right livelihood, not by family or wealth.
mn-123-p01.core_idea: Conduct, not family or wealth, purifies.

mn-123-p02.plain: Fellow monks plead with the gravely ill Channa not to take his own life. They want him to keep going, and promise to find him suitable food, medicine and a capable carer if he lacks them.
mn-123-p02.core_idea: Friends plead for a suffering companion to live.

sn-001-p01.plain: Time flies and nights slip by; the stages of life leave us one after another. Seeing the danger of death, do good deeds that will bring you joy.
sn-001-p01.core_idea: Life passes quickly; do good while you can.

sn-001-p02.plain: The monks don't grieve over the past or long for the future; they live on whatever each day brings, and so they look serene. Fools, longing for the future and grieving the past, wither like a cut green reed.
sn-001-p02.core_idea: Living in the present keeps you serene.

sn-001-p03.plain: Children bring you sorrow, and so do cattle. A person's attachments are their sorrow; without attachments there is no sorrow.
sn-001-p03.core_idea: Attachment is the source of sorrow.

sn-001-p04.plain: A mendicant should draw in their thoughts as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell. Independent, disturbing no one, at peace, they blame no one.
sn-001-p04.core_idea: Gather your thoughts in, like a tortoise.

sn-001-p05.plain: If you think of yourself as equal to others, better or worse, you'll end up arguing over it.
sn-001-p05.core_idea: Comparing yourself with others breeds dispute.

sn-001-p06.plain: Whoever wrongs an innocent, pure person finds the harm turns back on them, like fine dust thrown into the wind.
sn-001-p06.core_idea: Wronging the innocent rebounds on you.

sn-001-p08.plain: You don't need to guard the mind against everything, even if it isn't yet fully controlled. It only needs guarding from where bad things come.
sn-001-p08.core_idea: Guard the mind only where harm enters.

judge.issue: Reinterprets the obscure 'nor has the mind gained self-control' line.

sn-002-p01.plain: Keep company only with good people and stay close to them. Understanding the teaching of the good, you won't grieve among those who grieve.
sn-002-p01.core_idea: Keep good company and you won't grieve.

sn-002-p02.plain: When a miser holds back from giving out of fear, what they fear comes about anyway. The hunger and thirst they dread harm the fool in this world and the next.
sn-002-p02.core_idea: Stinginess brings the very want it fears.

sn-002-p03.plain: Those who share gladly from the little they have, like fellow travellers on a road, don't die among the dead. Some with little give happily while some with much won't give; a gift from little is multiplied a thousand times.
sn-002-p03.core_idea: Giving from little is worth a thousandfold.

sn-002-p04.plain: Gloom and suffering are both born of desire. Remove desire and gloom goes; remove gloom and suffering goes.
sn-002-p04.core_idea: Remove desire, and gloom and suffering go.

sn-002-p06.plain: Pretending to be someone you're not is like a cheating gambler enjoying stolen winnings. Say only what you will do, not what you won't; the wise can tell someone who talks without acting.
sn-002-p06.core_idea: Say only what you will actually do.

sn-002-p07.plain: If you refuse to forgive a mistake that has been confessed, holding hidden anger and hate, you stay trapped in enmity. The speaker doesn't approve of such enmity, and so forgives the mistake.
sn-002-p07.core_idea: Refusing to forgive keeps you trapped in enmity.

sn-002-p08.plain: Fools give themselves over to carelessness, but the wise guard their diligence as their greatest treasure.
sn-002-p08.core_idea: Diligence is the wise person's treasure.

sn-003-p01.plain: When your house burns, you save the useful pot, not the burnt one. The world burns with old age and death, so save by giving, since only what's given is saved. Enjoy what you have, and also give it away.
sn-003-p01.core_idea: What you give away is what you truly save.

judge.issue: Drops loss to bandits, rulers and fire, and the corpse cast off with possessions.

sn-004-p02.plain: Kill anger and you sleep at ease, free of sorrow. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, for when it's gone there is no sorrow.

sn-004-p04.plain: There are six holes through which your wealth drains away: laziness, negligence, lack of initiative, lack of restraint, sleepiness and sloth. Get rid of them completely.
sn-004-p04.core_idea: Laziness and carelessness drain your wealth.

sn-004-p05.plain: A person shouldn't give themselves away or abandon themselves. Speak when your words are good, but not when they are bad.
sn-004-p05.core_idea: Don't abandon yourself; speak only good words.

sn-004-p06.plain: Kāmada complains that the path is rough and hard. The Buddha replies that the noble keep going anyway: the ignoble fall headlong on rough ground, but the noble find the path smooth, because they stay smooth amid the rough.
sn-004-p06.core_idea: The noble stay smooth on a rough path.

sn-005-p02.plain: A spirit asks the Buddha whether he feels delight; he asks what he has gained. Whether he feels sorrow; he asks what he has lost. So he neither delights nor sorrows, and he agrees.
sn-005-p02.core_idea: Without gain or loss, neither delight nor sorrow.

sn-005-p03.plain: Fools act as their own worst enemies, doing wicked deeds that bear bitter fruit. It's not good to do something you'll weep over later; it is good to do what gladdens you afterward, as its effect stays with you.
sn-005-p03.core_idea: Do only what you won't regret later.

sn-005-p04.plain: A cart driver who leaves a smooth highway for a rough road frets once his axle breaks. Likewise, a dullard who leaves the good for what opposes it frets when caught in the jaws of death.
sn-005-p04.core_idea: Abandoning the good leads to regret at death.

sn-006-p03.plain: When a forest is burned black by fire, new shoots still spring up there again as the days and nights pass.
sn-006-p03.core_idea: New growth returns even after fire.

sn-007-p01.plain: Kings' fine chariots wear out, and this body grows old too. But the teaching of the good never ages, as the good tell each other.
sn-007-p01.core_idea: Bodies age, but the truth of the good doesn't.

sn-007-p02.plain: People who do bad things in deed, word or thought don't really love themselves, even if they say they do, because they treat themselves like an enemy.
sn-007-p02.core_idea: Doing wrong is treating yourself as an enemy.

sn-007-p03.plain: If you truly held yourself dear, you wouldn't tie yourself to wrongdoing, because happiness is hard to find for someone who does bad deeds.

sn-007-p04.plain: When death seizes you, what is truly yours, and what goes with you like a shadow? Only the good and bad you have done in this life; that is what you take with you.
sn-007-p04.core_idea: Only our deeds go with us at death.

sn-007-p05.plain: Restraint of body, speech and mind is good; restraint everywhere is good. A sincere person who is restrained in every way is said to be protected.
sn-007-p05.core_idea: Restraint in all things protects you.

sn-007-p06.plain: Searching every direction with the mind, you find no one dearer than yourself. Others hold themselves just as dear, so someone seeking self-knowledge would harm no one.
sn-007-p06.core_idea: Everyone holds themselves dear, so harm no one.

sn-007-p08.plain: You can't know a person by looks, so don't trust them at first sight. Undisciplined people pass as disciplined, like a clay earring or a gilded copper coin: corrupt inside, beautiful outside.

sn-008-p01.plain: A person who is always mindful and eats in moderation finds their discomfort easing; they age slowly and look after their life.
sn-008-p01.core_idea: Mindful, moderate eating eases and lengthens life.

sn-008-p03.plain: A killer breeds a killer, a conqueror a conqueror, an abuser abuse and a bully a bully. As deeds play out, the plunderer ends up plundered.
sn-008-p03.core_idea: What you do to others comes back to you.

sn-008-p05.plain: Like cool water in a deserted place that dries up undrunk, a bad person who gains wealth neither enjoys it nor gives it away.
sn-008-p05.core_idea: Hoarded wealth is wasted, like undrunk water.

sn-009-p01.plain: All beings are bound to die; death is their end and none is exempt. Just as every pot a potter makes, fired or unfired, will break, so all beings will die.
sn-009-p01.core_idea: All beings must die, as all pots break.

sn-009-p02.plain: Like huge mountains of rock closing in from every side, old age and death advance on all beings, high and low, crushing everything. No army, diplomacy or wealth can stop them.
sn-009-p02.core_idea: Old age and death crush everyone alike.

sn-010-p01.plain: The Buddha tells Māra that children and cattle bring sorrow. A person's attachments are their sorrow; without attachments there is no sorrow.
sn-010-p01.core_idea: Attachment is the source of sorrow.

sn-010-p02.plain: Days and nights rush past, and then life is cut short. Mortal life drains away like the water in tiny streams.

sn-010-p03.plain: Even if you shook the whole of Vulture's Peak, those who are truly freed and awakened would not be shaken.

sn-010-p04.plain: Even people with a dart in the heart get some sleep, so why not the Buddha, whose dart is drawn out? He lies down unafraid and untroubled, sees no decline for himself, and is full of kindness for all beings.
sn-010-p04.core_idea: With the dart removed, one rests in peace and kindness.

sn-011-p01.plain: Let us live very happily, owning nothing. We will feed on joy, like the radiant gods.
sn-011-p01.core_idea: Owning nothing, we can live on joy.

sn-011-p02.plain: Take a mountain of pure gold and double it, and it still wouldn't be enough for one person. Knowing this, live a moral life.
sn-011-p02.core_idea: No amount of wealth satisfies; live morally.

sn-011-p03.plain: Once someone has seen where suffering comes from, how could they lean toward sensual pleasures? Seeing attachment as a chain in the world, they would train to remove it.
sn-011-p03.core_idea: Seeing attachment as a chain, remove it.

sn-012-p01.plain: The nun Somā asks what difference being a woman makes when the mind is serene and knowledge is present as she rightly sees the Dhamma.
sn-012-p01.core_idea: Being a woman is no bar to wisdom.

sn-014-p01.plain: Everyone is born with an axe in their mouth, and fools cut themselves with it by saying bad things. Praising the blameworthy or blaming the praiseworthy is a losing hand you deal yourself; it never brings happiness.
sn-014-p01.core_idea: Careless words wound the one who speaks them.

sn-015-p01.plain: All conditioned things fall apart. Keep going with diligence.

sn-015-p02.plain: Conditioned things are impermanent; their nature is to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they cease, and their coming to rest is true bliss.
sn-015-p02.core_idea: The stilling of all that arises is bliss.

sn-015-p03.plain: Kill anger and you sleep at ease, free of sorrow. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, for when it's gone there is no sorrow.

sn-015-p04.plain: Getting angry at an angry person only makes things worse for you; not getting angry wins a hard battle. If you stay mindful and calm when someone is angry, you act for both your good and theirs.
sn-015-p04.core_idea: Staying calm with an angry person helps you both.

sn-015-p05.plain: The fool thinks they've won when they use harsh words. But for someone who understands, patient endurance is the real victory.
sn-015-p05.core_idea: Patient endurance, not harsh words, is victory.

sn-016-p02.plain: Asked who can untangle people tangled inside and out, the Buddha answers: a wise mendicant grounded in ethics, developing mind and wisdom, keen and alert, can untangle this tangle.
sn-016-p02.core_idea: Ethics, meditation and wisdom untangle the tangle.

sn-016-p03.plain: Don't ask about someone's birth; ask about their conduct, for fire can be born from any sticks. A steady sage, even from a low-class family, is a thoroughbred restrained by conscience.
sn-016-p03.core_idea: Judge people by conduct, not birth.

sn-016-p04.plain: The Buddha tells a fire-worshipping brahmin that conceit is his burden, anger his smoke and lies his ashes. The tongue is the ladle, the heart the fireplace, and a well-tamed self is a person's true light.
sn-016-p04.core_idea: A well-tamed self is your true light.

sn-016-p05.plain: The Buddha describes his farming: faith is his seed, effort his rain, wisdom his yoke and plough, conscience and mindfulness his tools. He guards body and speech, eats moderately, cuts with truth and finds release in gentleness.
sn-016-p05.core_idea: Spiritual practice is a kind of farming.

judge.issue: Compresses farming metaphor; drops mind as strap and goad.

sn-017-p01.plain: An old father laments that the sons he rejoiced over drove him out at their wives' urging. Calling him dear Dad, they proved monsters, and now, like an old horse led from its feed, he begs at others' homes.
sn-017-p01.core_idea: An aged father is cast out by his sons.

sn-017-p02.plain: Someone who loves to contradict, whose mind is tainted and aggressive, can't understand fine words. Once you let go of aggression, suspicion and resentment, you'll understand them.
sn-017-p02.core_idea: Let go of hostility to understand wise words.

sn-017-p03.plain: The Buddha has nothing to do in the jungle: his own inner jungle is cut at the root and withered. Free of its snarls and thorns, he enjoys solitude, having given up discontent.
sn-017-p03.core_idea: With the inner jungle cleared, solitude is joy.

sn-018-p01.plain: A monk sees it as his own misfortune that lust has left him dissatisfied. How could anyone else end his discontent and bring him satisfaction? He decides to do it himself.
sn-018-p01.core_idea: Only you can dispel your own discontent.

sn-018-p02.plain: Everything that has form, on earth, in the sky or deep below, wears out; all of it is impermanent. Those who examine themselves live having understood this.
sn-018-p02.core_idea: All that has form wears out.

sn-018-p03.plain: A man begs Ānanda to tell him how to quench his burning lust. Ānanda answers that his mind is on fire because of distorted perception; he should turn away from the attractive features of things that stir lust.

sn-018-p04.plain: Speak only words that don't hurt yourself or harm others; that is well-spoken speech. Speak pleasing words, gladly welcomed, that bring nothing bad to others. Truth is undying speech, and the good say the teaching rests on truth.
sn-018-p04.core_idea: Speak truthful words that harm no one.

sn-019-p01.plain: A deity tells a monk who sought seclusion that his mind still strays outward. Let go of longing for people, stay mindful, don't let sensual dust drag you down; shake it off, as a bird shakes off dirt.
sn-019-p01.core_idea: Shake off worldly longing like a bird shakes off dust.

judge.issue: Drops 'free of greed, happy' and giving up discontent.

sn-019-p02.plain: A dedicated ascetic must put up with many sounds and shouldn't be dismayed, because sounds don't defile you. If you startle at every little noise like a deer in the woods, you'll be called flighty and your practice won't succeed.
sn-019-p02.core_idea: Don't be startled by every noise.

sn-020-p01.plain: You are consumed by your thoughts because you apply your mind irrationally. Give up that irrationality and make sure your thoughts are sound.
sn-020-p01.core_idea: Unwise attention lets thoughts consume you.

sn-020-p02.plain: Two voices describe the same moment: the still of high noon, birds settled, the great forest humming. One finds it frightening; the other finds it delightful.
sn-020-p02.core_idea: The same moment can frighten or delight.

sn-020-p03.plain: To someone without blemish who always seeks purity, even the tiniest bit of evil looks as big as a storm cloud.
sn-020-p03.core_idea: To the pure, small faults look huge.

sn-020-p04.plain: Things always go well for the mindful, and each day is better for them, yet they aren't free of enmity. But someone who delights in harmlessness day and night, loving all living beings, has enmity for no one.
sn-020-p04.core_idea: Love for all beings ends all enmity.

sn-020-p05.plain: Don't do bad deeds, openly or secretly. If you have done one or are doing one now, you won't escape suffering, even if you fly away and flee.
sn-020-p05.core_idea: You can't flee the results of bad deeds.

sn-020-p06.plain: A spirit urges Anāthapiṇḍika on: a hundred elephants, horses, chariots and a hundred thousand jewelled maidens aren't worth a sixteenth of one step forward. Go forward, householder, and don't turn back!
sn-020-p06.core_idea: One step forward outweighs great riches.

sn-020-p07.plain: One who is fully at peace always sleeps at ease. Sensual pleasures slip off them; they are cool and unattached. Having cut off all clinging and removed the heart's stress, the peaceful sleep well.
sn-020-p07.core_idea: Without clinging, you sleep in peace.

sn-021-p01.plain: Asked about the best wealth, happiness, taste and life, the Buddha answers: faith is the best wealth, the teaching practised well brings happiness, truth is the sweetest taste, and the best life is lived by wisdom.
sn-021-p01.core_idea: Faith, truth and wisdom make the best life.

sn-021-p02.plain: Asked how to get past suffering, the answer is: faith carries you across the flood, diligence across the deluge, energy past suffering, and wisdom makes you pure.
sn-021-p02.core_idea: Faith, diligence, energy and wisdom carry you past suffering.

judge.issue: Frames whole answer as about suffering; drops the separate question of purification.

sn-021-p03.plain: You earn wealth by being responsible, doing what is fitting and working hard. Being truthful earns you a good name, and giving keeps your friends.
sn-021-p03.core_idea: Hard work earns wealth, truth reputation, giving friendship.

sn-021-p04.plain: The greatest patience is when a strong person puts up with a weak one; the weak have no choice. Foolish strength is really weakness, but someone strong and guarded by the teaching cannot be beaten.
sn-021-p04.core_idea: True patience is the strong bearing with the weak.

sn-022-p02.plain: A person should keep working until the goal is reached. For reaching a worthwhile goal, nothing is better than patience.
sn-022-p02.core_idea: Patience is the best way to reach a goal.

sn-022-p03.plain: You harvest whatever kind of seed you plant. Those who do good receive good, and those who do bad receive bad.

sn-023-p01.plain: Once anger is killed you sleep easily and sorrow goes. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, because then sorrow ends.
sn-023-p01.core_idea: Killing anger brings peaceful sleep and ends sorrow.

sn-023-p02.plain: My mind is not easily upset or pulled into turmoil. When anger comes it does not last, I do not speak harshly or boast, and I hold myself back for my own good.
sn-023-p02.core_idea: A steady mind lets anger pass without harsh words.

sn-023-p03.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants there are two kinds of fool: one who does not see their own mistake, and one who will not accept another's apology. The wise do both.
sn-023-p03.core_idea: Admit your mistakes and accept others' apologies.

judge.issue: "The wise do both" is vague; loses the explicit pairing of the two astute people.

sn-023-p04.plain: Do not let anger rule you, and do not get angry at angry people. The noble ones are always kind and harmless, and anger crushes bad people like a mountain.
sn-023-p04.core_idea: Do not let anger rule you.

sn-026-p01.plain: A lazy person lives miserably among bad qualities and misses their heart's highest goal; an energetic person lives happily and reaches it. The best is reached only by the best effort, never the worst.
sn-026-p01.core_idea: Energy, not laziness, reaches the heart's highest goal.

judge.issue: Adds "effort" to "the best is reached by the best".

sn-030-p01.plain: Whoever lies is full of fear and hostility in this life and lives to come, and suffers mental pain and sadness. Whoever stops lying is freed from that fear and hostility.
sn-030-p01.core_idea: Lying brings fear and pain; honesty calms it.

sn-032-p01.plain: A big fire goes out when no more fuel is added. In the same way, some things feed our grasping, and when you focus on their drawbacks, your craving stops.
sn-032-p01.core_idea: Starve craving by seeing the drawbacks of its fuel.

sn-033-p01.plain: What we call the mind or consciousness keeps arising as one thing and ending as another, day and night, like a monkey in a forest grabbing one branch after another.
sn-033-p01.core_idea: The mind jumps restlessly like a monkey between branches.

sn-035-p01.plain: A thirsty, exhausted man is offered a delicious-looking drink but told it is poisoned and will bring death or deadly pain, so he quenches his thirst another way. In the same way, past ascetics saw pleasant things as impermanent, suffering, not-self, diseased and dangerous, and gave up craving.
sn-035-p01.core_idea: Refuse pleasant things that bring lasting harm.

extension.text: Suppose there was a bronze goblet of beverage that had a nice color, aroma, and flavor. But it was mixed with poison. Then along comes a man struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. They’d say to him: ‘Here, my man, this bronze goblet of beverage has a nice color, aroma, and flavor. But it’s mixed with poison. Drink it if you like. If you drink it, its nice color, aroma, and flavor will refresh you. But drinking it will result in death or deadly pain.’ Then that man might think: ‘I can allay my thirst with a fermented drink of beer, buttermilk, salt lassi, or salted infusion. But in any case, I shouldn’t drink that beverage, for it would be for my lasting harm and suffering.’ He’d put that beverage down. After appraisal, he wouldn’t drink it, and it wouldn’t result in death or deadly pain. In the same way, there were ascetics and brahmins of the past who saw the things that seem nice and pleasant in the world as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self, as diseased, and as dangerous. They gave up craving.

sn-035-p01.plain_v1: A thirsty man is offered a delicious drink that is laced with poison and would kill him. He thinks it over, chooses another drink, and leaves the poisoned one alone, avoiding death.

judge_v1.issue: Drops the point: ascetics saw pleasant things as dangerous and gave up craving.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Omits the point: past ascetics saw pleasures as dangerous and gave up craving.

sn-038-p01.plain: A torch dropped in dry grass does no harm if quickly put out. Likewise, if a seeker quickly drops a corrupt thought, they live happily now and can expect a good rebirth after death.
sn-038-p01.core_idea: Put out a bad thought quickly, like a dropped torch.

sn-038-p02.plain: People with low convictions gather with others like them, and people with good convictions gather with others like them.
sn-038-p02.core_idea: People are drawn to those who share their convictions.

sn-039-p01.plain: Mixing with people tangles you up. Like clinging to a small log at sea, you sink if you rely on a lazy person, so avoid them and live with the noble, devoted and energetic.
sn-039-p01.core_idea: Avoid lazy company; keep company with the energetic and wise.

judge.issue: Drops "cut off by being aloof" and the secluded who practise absorption.

sn-040-p01.plain: Over countless lives you have shed more tears than all the water in the four oceans, grieving the deaths of family, losses of every kind, and being parted from those you love.
sn-040-p01.core_idea: Across endless lives your tears outweigh the oceans.

sn-041-p01.plain: When you see someone suffering and in distress, remind yourself that over the long round of lives, you too have been through exactly the same.
sn-041-p01.core_idea: You too have suffered as others suffer.

sn-042-p02.plain: Anyone with faith, conscience, prudence, energy and wisdom in good qualities will only grow in them, day and night, just as the waxing moon keeps growing in beauty and size.
sn-042-p02.core_idea: Good qualities grow steadily like the waxing moon.

sn-044-p01.plain: Possessions, honour and popularity are harsh and bitter, and block the way to the highest freedom. So train yourself to give them up and not let them fill your mind.
sn-044-p01.core_idea: Wealth, honour and fame are obstacles to freedom.

sn-044-p02.plain: A true person's meditation stays steady whether they are honoured or ignored. They keep meditating with clear understanding and rejoice in the end of clinging.
sn-044-p02.core_idea: Honour or neglect cannot shake a true person.

judge.issue: Drops abiding in the immeasurables; "subtle view and discernment" loosened.

sn-045-p01.plain: Just as a banana plant, bamboo and reed are destroyed by their own fruit, honour destroys a bad person.

judge.issue: Drops the mule-and-pregnancy image.

sn-046-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that giving huge gifts of rice three times a day is less fruitful than developing a loving heart even for a moment, the time it takes to milk a cow.
sn-046-p01.core_idea: A moment of love outweighs great gifts.

sn-047-p01.plain: We will be grateful and thankful, and never forget even a small kindness done for us.
sn-047-p01.core_idea: Remember even small kindnesses with gratitude.

sn-048-p01.plain: Extinguishment, freedom from all suffering, cannot be reached by someone slack or weak in effort.
sn-048-p01.core_idea: Freedom from suffering demands strong effort.

sn-048-p02.plain: Geese, herons, peacocks, elephants and deer differ in size, yet all fear the lion. Among people too, a small person who is wise is truly great, not a fool with a fine body.
sn-048-p02.core_idea: Wisdom, not size, makes a person great.

sn-048-p03.plain: Why are you angry, Tissa? Do not be. It is better not to be angry, because the spiritual life is lived to remove anger, pride and contempt.
sn-048-p03.core_idea: The spiritual life exists to remove anger.

sn-048-p04.plain: Truly living alone means letting go of the past, giving up the future, and ending desire and greed for life in the present.
sn-048-p04.core_idea: Living alone means releasing past, future and present craving.

sn-048-p05.plain: An old, sick man asks the Buddha for advice. The Buddha agrees the body is frail and says to train like this: though my body is sick, my mind will be healthy.
sn-048-p05.core_idea: Though the body is ailing, keep the mind healthy.

sn-049-p01.plain: Arguing with people means engaging in talk like: you don't understand, I do; you're wrong, I'm right; your view is refuted, get out of that if you can.
sn-049-p01.core_idea: Quarrelling is the contest of 'I'm right, you're wrong'.

sn-050-p01.plain: Carrying the burden is suffering, and putting it down is happiness. Someone who lays down the heavy burden without picking up another, and pulls out craving by the root, is satisfied and at peace.
sn-050-p01.core_idea: Laying down the burden of craving brings peace.

sn-051-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to give up what is not theirs, because letting it go will bring them wellbeing and happiness.
sn-051-p01.core_idea: Let go of what is not yours.

sn-052-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to be their own island and refuge, relying on nothing else, and to make the teaching their island and refuge.
sn-052-p01.core_idea: Be your own refuge, with the teaching as refuge.

sn-053-p01.plain: An untaught person worries over things not worth worrying about, fearing what might not be or not be theirs. A learned disciple of the noble ones does not worry about such things.
sn-053-p01.core_idea: The wise do not worry about losing what isn't theirs.

sn-054-p01.plain: When you cling, you are caught by Māra; when you do not cling, you are free of the Wicked One.
sn-054-p01.core_idea: Clinging binds you; letting go frees you.

sn-055-p01.plain: Give up desire for anything that does not last.
sn-055-p01.core_idea: Do not desire what is impermanent.

sn-055-p02.plain: How happy the perfected ones are! They have no craving, no sense of 'I am', and no delusion. Their minds are calm and clear, nothing in the world clings to them, and they are pure.
sn-055-p02.core_idea: The perfected ones are happy, free of craving and ego.

judge.issue: Drops "manifesting divinity"; imperturbability softened to calm.

sn-056-p01.plain: Living on alms is the lowest way of life, and people mock beggars. Yet sincere men choose it, not from fear or debt, but because they are overwhelmed by suffering and hope to end it entirely.
sn-056-p01.core_idea: Seekers embrace poverty to end suffering.

sn-059-p01.plain: Both before and now, all I teach is suffering and the ending of suffering.
sn-059-p01.core_idea: The teaching is suffering and its ending.

sn-059-p02.plain: The Buddha tells Vakkali there is no point in seeing his decaying body. Whoever sees the teaching sees the Buddha, and whoever sees the Buddha sees the teaching.
sn-059-p02.core_idea: To see the teaching is to see the Buddha.

sn-059-p03.plain: Like a lamp that goes out when its oil and wick run out, a dying person knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that all feeling, no longer relished, will simply cool.
sn-059-p03.core_idea: At death, unrelished feeling simply cools like a spent lamp.

sn-060-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants he does not argue with the world; the world argues with him. When your words agree with the teaching, you have no quarrel with anyone.
sn-060-p01.core_idea: Speak in line with truth and quarrel with no one.

sn-060-p02.plain: A lotus grows in water yet rises above it with no water clinging to it. In the same way, though born and raised in the world, the Buddha lives above it, untouched by it.
sn-060-p02.core_idea: Live in the world untouched by it, like a lotus.

sn-060-p03.plain: A bubble on rainwater forms and bursts at once; looked at closely it is empty and without substance. A mendicant who looks closely at feeling sees it is just as empty.
sn-060-p03.core_idea: Feelings are as empty as water bubbles.

sn-061-p01.plain: The Buddha taught that the body is like foam, feeling like a bubble, perception like a mirage, choices like a banana plant and consciousness like an illusion: examined closely, all are hollow.
sn-061-p01.core_idea: Body and mind are hollow when examined closely.

sn-061-p02.plain: Regularly look at your own mind and recognise it has long been stained by greed, hate and delusion. Beings are corrupted when the mind is corrupted, and purified when the mind is purified.
sn-061-p02.core_idea: Purity and corruption begin in the mind.

sn-062-p01.plain: A mason sees his adze handle wearing away but cannot tell how much went each day, only that it is worn. Likewise, a committed mendicant cannot measure daily progress, but knows the defilements are wearing away.
sn-062-p01.core_idea: Spiritual progress is unseen day to day but real.

sn-065-p01.plain: Children treasure sandcastles while they still want them, then smash them once the desire is gone. In the same way, break apart body, feeling, perception, choices and consciousness, and work to end craving, which is extinguishment.
sn-065-p01.core_idea: Smash attachments like outgrown sandcastles to end craving.

sn-072-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the eye does not last, and what does not last is suffering and not self. See it truly: this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.
sn-072-p01.core_idea: The impermanent is not mine, not me, not self.

sn-073-p01.plain: Whatever you imagine a thing to be, or imagine as 'mine', turns into something else. The world clings to existence and delights only in it, yet it keeps changing.
sn-073-p01.core_idea: Whatever we cling to as ours keeps changing.

sn-074-p01.plain: There are attractive, pleasing sights. If a mendicant does not welcome or cling to them, delight in them stops, and when that delight stops, the Buddha says, suffering stops.
sn-074-p01.core_idea: Ending delight in pleasures ends suffering.

sn-076-p01.plain: The Buddha tells Ānanda the world is called empty because it is empty of a self or anything belonging to a self: the senses, their objects, and every feeling are empty in this way.
sn-076-p01.core_idea: The world is empty of self.

sn-076-p02.plain: Whoever depends on things wavers; whoever does not depend is still. Stillness brings calm, calm ends leaning and coming and going, and with that there is no dying, rebirth, or any life: this is the end of suffering.
sn-076-p02.core_idea: Without dependence there is stillness and an end of suffering.

judge.issue: "No ... any life" overstates; passage says no this life, next, or between.

sn-076-p03.plain: The Buddha asks Puṇṇa what he will think if the rough people he is going to live among insult him. Puṇṇa says he will think them kind, because at least they do not hit him.
sn-076-p03.core_idea: Meet insult with gratitude that it is not worse.

sn-077-p01.plain: When you see pleasant and unpleasant sights, let go of all desire for the pleasant, without hating what you dislike.
sn-077-p01.core_idea: Desire nothing pleasant; hate nothing unpleasant.

sn-077-p02.plain: Whether a smell is sweet or foul, or a taste sweet or bitter, drop aversion to the unpleasant and do not give in to desire or attachment for the pleasant.
sn-077-p02.core_idea: Meet pleasant and unpleasant senses without craving or aversion.

sn-078-p01.plain: When you see something and fix on its pleasant side, you lose mindfulness and cling with desire. Feelings multiply, greed and cruelty damage the mind, and piling up suffering this way, you are far from extinguishment.
sn-078-p01.core_idea: Clinging to pleasant sights piles up suffering.

sn-078-p02.plain: Seeing something with mindfulness, you feel no desire and do not cling. Even while experiencing it you wear suffering away instead of piling it up, and so you are close to extinguishment.

sn-080-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that the end of the world cannot be known, seen or reached by travelling, yet suffering cannot end without reaching the end of the world.
sn-080-p01.core_idea: The world's end is reached within, not by travel.

sn-081-p01.plain: Eating in moderation means a mendicant reflects that food is not for fun or vanity, but only to keep the body going, avoid harm and support spiritual practice, easing hunger without creating new discomfort.
sn-081-p01.core_idea: Eat to sustain the body, not for indulgence.

sn-082-p01.plain: A calm, clear, untroubled mind that is kind to all creatures is the path to becoming divine.
sn-082-p01.core_idea: A calm, kind mind is the path to the divine.

sn-082-p02.plain: A mendicant who sees something does not hold on to it if it is pleasant or dislike it if it is unpleasant. They live mindful of the body, with a boundless heart.
sn-082-p02.core_idea: Neither grasp the pleasant nor resent the unpleasant.

sn-083-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that gods and humans love and enjoy sights, but when those sights fade and end, they suffer.
sn-083-p01.core_idea: Loving what fades leads to suffering.

sn-083-p02.plain: What other people call happiness, the noble ones call suffering, and what others call suffering, the noble ones know to be happiness.
sn-083-p02.core_idea: The wise see happiness and suffering in reverse.

sn-083-p03.plain: Here are trees to sit under and empty huts. The Buddha urges the mendicants to meditate, not to be careless, and not to regret it later: this is his instruction.
sn-083-p03.core_idea: Meditate now, so you will not regret it later.

sn-085-p01.plain: The eye is an ocean whose currents are sights. Whoever overcomes those currents, with all their waves and dangers, has crossed over and stands on solid ground on the far shore.
sn-085-p01.core_idea: Master the currents of the senses to cross over.

sn-085-p02.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that a monk or nun who still has greed, hate and delusion is overwhelmed even by trivial sights, let alone compelling ones, because those roots remain.
sn-085-p02.core_idea: While greed remains, even small sights overwhelm the mind.

sn-086-p01.plain: Two oxen joined by a yoke are not each other's yoke; the yoke binds them. Likewise the eye and sights do not bind each other; what binds is the desire and greed arising between them.
sn-086-p01.core_idea: Desire, not the senses, is what binds us.

sn-087-p01.plain: Eating in moderation means a mendicant eats only to sustain the body and support practice, not for pleasure, like putting ointment on a wound only to heal it, or oiling an axle only to carry a load.
sn-087-p01.core_idea: Eat only to sustain the body, as ointment heals.

sn-088-p01.plain: Someone in a thorny thicket moves carefully and mindfully to avoid the thorns. In the same way, in the Noble One's training, whatever in the world seems nice and pleasant is called a thorn.
sn-088-p01.core_idea: Pleasant things are thorns on the spiritual path.

sn-089-p01.plain: Asked what a parrot tree is like, different people describe it as blackish, reddish, flaking or leafy, each rightly for the time they saw it. In the same way, those true persons each answered according to what they focused on when their vision was purified.
sn-089-p01.core_idea: Different true answers come from different vantage points.

extension.text: “Mendicant, suppose a person had never seen a parrot tree before. They’d go up to someone who had seen a parrot tree and ask them, ‘My man, what’s a parrot tree like?’ They’d say, ‘A parrot tree is blackish, like a charred stump.’ Now, at that time a parrot tree may well have been just as that person saw it. Not content with that answer, that person would go up to a series of other people and receive the following answers: ‘A parrot tree is reddish, like a scrap of meat.’ ‘A parrot tree has flaking bark and burst pods, like a lebbeck tree.’ ‘A parrot tree has luxuriant, shady foliage, like a banyan.’ Now, at each of those times a parrot tree may well have been just as those people saw them. In the same way, those true persons each answered according to what they were focused on when their vision was well purified.

sn-089-p01.plain_v1: A person asks different people what a parrot tree looks like and gets different answers, black, red, pod-laden, leafy, each true of the tree at the time that person saw it.

judge_v1.issue: Drops the application: true persons answered according to their focus.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Omits the point: true persons answered by their focus with purified vision.

sn-090-p01.plain: The 'abyss' is really painful bodily feeling. An untaught person facing pain wails and falls into confusion, finding no footing; a learned disciple of the noble ones meets pain without lament and finds firm footing.
sn-090-p01.core_idea: Meeting pain calmly gives footing in the abyss.

sn-090-p02.plain: If you cannot bear painful bodily feelings and tremble and wail at them, you will not find your footing in the abyss. If you can endure them without trembling, you will.
sn-090-p02.core_idea: Enduring pain without trembling gives you footing.

sn-090-p03.plain: When an untaught person feels bodily pain and adds grief and confusion, they feel two pains, physical and mental, like someone shot by one arrow and then a second.
sn-090-p03.core_idea: Mental distress is a second arrow after pain.

sn-090-p04.plain: A learned person who has understood the teaching sees this world and the next clearly. Desirable things do not stir their mind, and undesirable things do not repel them.
sn-090-p04.core_idea: The wise are unmoved by liking and disliking.

sn-091-p01.plain: Like a lamp that goes out when oil and wick run out, a dying mendicant knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that every feeling, no longer enjoyed, will simply cool.
sn-091-p01.core_idea: At death, feelings no longer enjoyed simply cool.

sn-091-p02.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that winds of every kind blow from all directions, dusty or clean, cool or warm, weak or strong. In the same way, pleasant, painful and neutral feelings arise in the body.
sn-091-p02.core_idea: Feelings come and go like winds.

sn-091-p03.plain: A guest house takes in travellers from every direction and of every class. In the same way, pleasant, painful and neutral feelings come and stay in this body.
sn-091-p03.core_idea: The body hosts feelings like a guest house.

sn-092-p01.plain: The Buddha says he has explained feelings in many ways. Those who will not accept what is well said will quarrel and wound each other; those who accept it will live in harmony, blending like milk and water.
sn-092-p01.core_idea: Accepting what is well said brings harmony, not quarrels.

sn-094-p01.plain: Sāriputta says that in this path, going forth is hard; once gone forth, being content is hard; once content, practising the teaching is hard. But whoever practises it will soon be perfected.
sn-094-p01.core_idea: Each stage is hard, but true practice soon succeeds.

sn-098-p01.plain: Someone who has given up greed, hate and delusion is not annoyed by others and does not show annoyance, so they are seen as gentle. That is why some people are considered gentle.
sn-098-p01.core_idea: Gentleness comes from giving up greed, hate and delusion.

sn-099-p01.plain: Someone reflects: the Buddha condemns lying, I have lied, that was wrong and I regret it, but I cannot undo it. So they stop lying from now on. That is how to leave a bad deed behind.
sn-099-p01.core_idea: Admit the wrong, stop repeating it, and move past it.

sn-100-p01.plain: A chief admits he worries all day about his son living far away, and would grieve terribly if harm came to him. The Buddha says this shows that all suffering is rooted in desire.
sn-100-p01.core_idea: Desire is the root of suffering.

sn-100-p02.plain: One who has gone forth should avoid two extremes: indulging in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, and tormenting oneself, which is painful and pointless. The Buddha found the middle way between them, leading to peace and awakening.
sn-100-p02.core_idea: Avoid both indulgence and self-torment: take the middle way.

sn-102-p02.plain: Joy arises in them, and joy grows into rapture. With a rapturous mind the body becomes calm, a calm body feels bliss, and in bliss the mind settles into deep meditation.
sn-102-p02.core_idea: Joy leads step by step to deep meditative calm.

sn-105-p01.plain: Ānanda says good friends and companions are half the spiritual life. The Buddha corrects him: good friends and companions are the whole of the spiritual life.
sn-105-p01.core_idea: Good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.

sn-106-p01.plain: Right speech means avoiding speech that is false, divisive, harsh or pointless.
sn-106-p01.core_idea: Right speech avoids lies, slander, harshness and idle talk.

sn-107-p01.plain: A pot without a stand tips over easily, but a pot on a stand is hard to knock over. The mind is the same: without support it is easily upset, with support it is hard to upset.
sn-107-p01.core_idea: A mind with firm support is hard to upset.

sn-107-p03.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that just as dawn comes before sunrise, good friendship comes before the noble eightfold path.
sn-107-p03.core_idea: Good friendship is the dawn of the spiritual path.

sn-109-p01.plain: Every animal's footprint fits inside an elephant's, so the elephant's is called the greatest. In the same way, all good qualities are rooted in diligence and meet in it, so diligence is the best.
sn-109-p01.core_idea: Diligence is the root of all good qualities.

sn-109-p02.plain: A tree leaning east, when cut at the root, falls east. In the same way, a mendicant who develops the noble eightfold path leans and inclines toward extinguishment.
sn-109-p02.core_idea: You fall the way you lean.

extension.text: “Mendicants, suppose a tree slants, slopes, and inclines to the east. If it was cut off at the root, where would it fall?” “Sir, it would fall in the direction that it slants, slopes, and inclines.” “In the same way, a mendicant who develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path slants, slopes, and inclines to extinguishment.

sn-109-p02.plain_v1: The Buddha asks the mendicants where a tree leaning east would fall if cut at the root. They answer: in the direction it leans.

judge_v1.issue: Drops the point: the path inclines the mendicant toward extinguishment.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Omits the point: the eightfold path inclines a mendicant to extinguishment.

sn-110-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants there are three kinds of comparing oneself: thinking 'I'm better', 'I'm equal', or 'I'm worse'.
sn-110-p01.core_idea: Better, equal or worse: all comparison is conceit.

sn-110-p02.plain: What makes ill will arise and grow? Dwelling again and again, unwisely, on what we find repellent feeds ill will and makes it grow.
sn-110-p02.core_idea: Dwelling on what repels you feeds ill will.

sn-111-p01.plain: A mendicant sees a pleasing sight without desire or greed, and an unpleasant one without dismay, irritation or anger. Either way, their mind and body stay steady, settled and free.
sn-111-p01.core_idea: Stay steady whether sights please or displease.

sn-112-p01.plain: The Buddha asks the sick Kassapa if his pain is easing; Kassapa says it is terrible and growing. The Buddha reminds him of the seven awakening factors he has rightly taught, which when developed lead to direct knowledge, awakening and extinguishment.
sn-112-p01.core_idea: Honestly admitting that pain is growing.

extension.text: “I hope you’re keeping well, Kassapa, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.” “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.” “Kassapa, I’ve rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

sn-112-p01.plain_v1: The Buddha asks the sick Kassapa if he is getting better and his pain easing. Kassapa answers honestly that he is not well: his pain is terrible and growing worse.

judge_v1.issue: Drops the Buddha's answer about the seven awakening factors; only the complaint remains.

judge_v1_rejudged.issue: Omits the Buddha's teaching on the seven awakening factors, the passage's conclusion.

sn-113-p01.plain: Gold mixed with iron, copper, tin, lead or silver is brittle and dull. In the same way, sensual desire, ill will, drowsiness, restlessness and doubt make the mind brittle and unable to settle in meditation.
sn-113-p01.core_idea: Five hindrances corrupt the mind like impurities in gold.

sn-114-p01.plain: What starves ill will, so it does not arise or grow? The heart's release by love: dwelling on it again and again, wisely, starves ill will.

sn-114-p02.plain: When the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop tranquility, deep meditation and equanimity, because these easily settle a restless mind.
sn-114-p02.core_idea: Calm a restless mind with tranquility and equanimity.

sn-115-p01.plain: In a muddy bowl of water in the dark, you cannot see your reflection. Likewise, when your heart is sunk in doubt, you cannot see what is good for yourself, for others, or for both.
sn-115-p01.core_idea: Doubt clouds the mind like muddy water.

sn-115-p02.plain: In a clear bowl of water in the light, you see your reflection plainly. Likewise, when your heart is free of doubt, you clearly see what is good for yourself, for others, and for both.
sn-115-p02.core_idea: A mind free of doubt sees clearly, like clear water.

sn-116-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the direct path to purify beings, get past sorrow and tears, end pain and sadness, and reach extinguishment.
sn-116-p01.core_idea: Mindfulness is the direct path beyond sorrow.

sn-117-p01.plain: Careful monkeys see the sticky tar trap and keep away. A reckless monkey grabs it and gets stuck, then grabs with his other hand to free himself and gets stuck again.
sn-117-p01.core_idea: Struggling with a trap only entangles you further.

sn-118-p03.plain: The Buddha tells Sāriputta that someone whose mind is free is a great person, and someone whose mind is not free is not.

sn-118-p04.plain: Ānanda grieves for Sāriputta, who guided and counselled him, taught, encouraged and inspired him, never tired of teaching the Dhamma, and supported his companions on the path.
sn-118-p04.core_idea: Grieving a beloved teacher and guide.

judge.issue: Adds that Ananda grieves; the passage only praises Sariputta as adviser.

sn-118-p05.plain: The Buddha reminds Ānanda that he taught we must be parted from everyone and everything we love. Whatever is born and made must wear out; it cannot be otherwise.
sn-118-p05.core_idea: All we love must pass; nothing made can last.

sn-119-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants the assembly feels empty now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have passed away. It never felt empty before, and wherever they stayed, he had no worry.
sn-119-p01.core_idea: Even the Buddha feels the emptiness of loss.

judge.issue: Renders 'fully quenched' as 'passed away', losing the spiritual sense.

sn-119-p02.plain: You look after others by looking after yourself through meditation, and look after yourself by looking after others through patience, harmlessness, love and sympathy. Caring for yourself and caring for others go together.
sn-119-p02.core_idea: Caring for yourself and caring for others go together.

judge.issue: Drops that mindfulness meditation is cultivated for both self and others.

sn-120-p01.plain: A mendicant is aware when they know their feelings, thoughts and perceptions as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away.
sn-120-p01.core_idea: Awareness is watching experiences arise, stay and pass.

sn-123-p01.plain: Sadness arises from something experienced as sad. When you are sad, you know that you are sad, and when its cause ends, you know the sadness has ended too.
sn-123-p01.core_idea: Know sadness as it arises and as it ends.

sn-124-p01.plain: When young you are bound to grow old, when healthy to fall ill, when alive to die. The skin loses its brightness, the limbs wrinkle, the body stoops, and the senses decline.
sn-124-p01.core_idea: Youth, health and life all give way to decline.

sn-124-p02.plain: Curse this wretched old age that makes the lovely body ugly and wears it down. Even if you live a hundred years, you will still die; death spares no one.
sn-124-p02.core_idea: Old age wears us down and death spares no one.

sn-125-p01.plain: After trying, remembering, meditating and reflecting wisely again and again, a noble disciple becomes confident: once I only heard of these things, now I experience and see them directly.
sn-125-p01.core_idea: Repeated practice turns hearsay into direct experience.

sn-126-p01.plain: The four right efforts are working hard to keep bad qualities from arising, to give up bad qualities that have arisen, to make good qualities arise, and to keep good ones growing to fullness.
sn-126-p01.core_idea: Prevent and abandon bad; grow and keep good.

sn-129-p01.plain: Enthusiasm is too slack when it comes with laziness, and too tense when it comes with restlessness.
sn-129-p01.core_idea: Effort fails when too slack or too tense.

sn-131-p01.plain: Asked how he keeps physical pain from taking over his mind, the gravely ill Anuruddha says he keeps his mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.
sn-131-p01.core_idea: Mindfulness keeps pain from occupying the mind.

judge.issue: Adds 'gravely ill', which the passage does not state.

sn-132-p01.plain: To practise mindfulness of breathing, a mendicant sits somewhere quiet, straight and cross-legged, and simply breathes in and out mindfully, knowing when each breath is heavy or light.
sn-132-p01.core_idea: Sit still and know each breath as it comes.

sn-133-p01.plain: Like a lamp going out when its oil and wick are spent, a dying person knows the end of body and life is near, and understands that all feeling, no longer enjoyed, will simply cool.
sn-133-p01.core_idea: At death, feelings no longer enjoyed simply cool.

sn-133-p02.plain: As an unseasonal storm settles summer dust at once, meditation on breathing, when developed, is peaceful and blissful, and settles bad qualities the moment they arise.
sn-133-p02.core_idea: Mindful breathing settles bad states like rain settles dust.

sn-135-p01.plain: Those with faith, good conduct, confidence and a clear view of the truth eventually reach happiness, the goal of the spiritual life.
sn-135-p01.core_idea: Faith, ethics and insight lead in time to happiness.

sn-136-p01.plain: A noble disciple reflects: I want to live and be happy and I hate pain, so I would not want to be killed. Others feel the same. How can I do to them what I would hate done to me?
sn-136-p01.core_idea: Do not inflict on others what you would hate yourself.

sn-137-p01.plain: When a pot of ghee breaks underwater, the shards sink but the ghee rises. Likewise, when someone long steeped in faith, ethics, learning, generosity and wisdom dies, the body decays and is eaten, but the mind rises higher.
sn-137-p01.core_idea: A good mind rises when the body perishes.

sn-138-p01.plain: Whoever has firm faith in the Buddha, good conduct loved by the noble ones, confidence in the Saṅgha and right view is truly rich; their life is not wasted. So the wise should devote themselves to these.
sn-138-p01.core_idea: Faith, ethics and right view make a life rich.

sn-140-p01.plain: Living diligently, joy arises and grows into rapture. Rapture calms the body, a calm body feels bliss, bliss settles the mind in deep meditation, and then the truth becomes clear.
sn-140-p01.core_idea: Diligence leads through joy and calm to clarity.

sn-140-p02.plain: Someone who seeks merit and is grounded in good develops the path to freedom from death. Having reached the heart of the teaching and delighting in ending, they do not tremble when the King of Death approaches.
sn-140-p02.core_idea: One who has realised the teaching does not fear death.

sn-141-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants not to think bad thoughts, such as sensual, malicious or cruel ones, because they do not help the spiritual life or lead to peace, insight and awakening.
sn-141-p01.core_idea: Avoid thoughts that do not lead to peace.

sn-141-p02.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants not to get into arguments of the 'I'm right, you're wrong, your view is refuted' kind, because such talk does not help the spiritual life or lead to peace and awakening.
sn-141-p02.core_idea: Don't argue about who is right; it leads nowhere.

sn-142-p01.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to avoid two extremes: indulging in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, and tormenting oneself, which is painful and pointless. He found the middle way, leading to peace and awakening.
sn-142-p01.core_idea: The middle way avoids indulgence and self-torment.

sn-142-p02.plain: This is the noble truth of suffering: birth, ageing, illness and death are suffering; being with what you dislike, parted from what you like, and not getting what you want are suffering.
sn-142-p02.core_idea: Life's losses and frustrations are the truth of suffering.

sn-143-p01.plain: Holding a few leaves, the Buddha says that what he has taught is like those few leaves compared with the forest: he knows far more, but leaves it unsaid because it does not help the spiritual life.
sn-143-p01.core_idea: Teach only what helps; the rest is left unsaid.

sn-144-p01.plain: A deep-rooted pillar cannot be shaken by storms from any side. In the same way, those who truly understand suffering, its origin, its ending and the path do not look to other teachers, thinking they must know better.
sn-144-p01.core_idea: Those who truly understand stand firm, needing no other's authority.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p01.plain: The poet tells God: you have made me endless, emptying and refilling this fragile vessel with new life, playing new melodies through me. Your touch fills my heart with joy, and your gifts keep pouring into my small hands.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p01.core_idea: God endlessly refills and plays through a small life.

judge.issue: Drops 'such is thy pleasure' and 'still there is room to fill'.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p02.plain: When God asks the poet to sing, his heart nearly bursts with pride and tears come as he looks at God's face. All that is harsh in his life melts into harmony, and his worship flies like a happy bird.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p02.core_idea: Singing for God turns life's discord into harmony.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p03.plain: The poet vows to God, the life of his life, to keep body pure, thoughts truthful and heart loving, since God touches, enlightens and dwells in him, and to show God in his deeds, since God gives him strength.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p03.core_idea: Live purely because God dwells within you.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p04.plain: The poet asks God for a moment to sit beside him; work can wait. Away from God his heart finds no rest and work is endless toil. Summer has come: now is the time to sit quietly with God.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p04.core_idea: Pause from work to sit quietly with God.

fix.display_text:
I ask for a moment’s indulgence to sit by thy side. The works that I have in hand I will finish afterwards.

Away from the sight of thy face my heart knows no rest nor respite, and my work becomes an endless toil in a shoreless sea of toil.

Today the summer has come at my window with its sighs and murmurs; and the bees are plying their minstrelsy at the court of the flowering grove.

Now it is time to sit quiet, face to face with thee, and to sing dedication of life in this silent and overflowing leisure.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p05.plain: The poet asks God to pick the little flower of his life now, before it wilts. Though pale and faintly scented, let it serve God, for he fears the time for offering will pass.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p05.core_idea: Offer your life now, before the time passes.

judge.issue: Drops the plea to honour it 'with a touch of pain'; adds 'of his life'.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p06.plain: The poet's song has dropped its ornaments, which would come between him and God. His poet's pride dies; sitting at God's feet, he asks only for a simple life, like a reed flute for God to fill.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p06.core_idea: A simple life lets God's music through.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p07.plain: A child in fine robes and jewels cannot enjoy play, afraid to get dirty or move. Finery is no gain if it shuts you off from the earth's healthy dust and the shared life of ordinary people.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p07.core_idea: Finery that cuts you off from life is worthless.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p08.plain: Carrying yourself on your own shoulders is foolish, like begging at your own door. Leave your burdens with the one who bears all, without regret. Desire defiles what it touches; accept only what sacred love offers.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p08.core_idea: Lay your burdens down and accept only what love gives.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p09.plain: The poet tells God that God's feet rest among the poorest, lowliest and lost. His bowing, his pride and his heart cannot reach down to where God walks humbly and keeps company with the companionless.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p09.core_idea: God is found among the poorest and the lost.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p10.plain: Stop chanting in a dark, shut temple: God is not there. God is with the farmer and road-builder, covered in dust, bound with all of creation. Come out and stand with God in toil and sweat.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p10.core_idea: God is found in honest labour, not closed temples.

fix.display_text:
Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!

He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones. He is with them in sun and in shower, and his garment is covered with dust. Put off thy holy mantle and even like him come down on the dusty soil!

Deliverance? Where is this deliverance to be found? Our master himself has joyfully taken upon him the bonds of creation; he is bound with us all for ever.

Come out of thy meditations and leave aside thy flowers and incense! What harm is there if thy clothes become tattered and stained? Meet him and stand by him in toil and in sweat of thy brow.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p11.plain: The longest journey leads nearest to God, as the hardest training leads to the simplest tune. You must knock at every stranger's door to reach your own. After searching far, the poet closes his eyes and finds God here.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p11.core_idea: The longest search leads back home to God within.

judge.issue: Drops the final stanza: the cry 'Oh, where?' becoming the assurance 'I am!'

tagore-gitanjali-001-p12.plain: The song I came to sing is still unsung. I have spent my days tuning my instrument, and the time and words were never right. There is only the ache of longing, like a bud that has not opened.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p12.core_idea: The ache of a life's song still unsung.

tagore-gitanjali-001-p13.plain: The poet tells God: my desires are many, but you have always saved me by refusing them. That firm mercy is making me worthy of your simple, great gifts, sky, light, body, life and mind, and of your full acceptance.
tagore-gitanjali-001-p13.core_idea: God's refusals are a mercy that saves us.

judge.issue: Drops God hiding cruelly and the perils of overmuch and uncertain desire.
